title: Mossbourne and Natural Justice
author: Greg Ashman
source: Filling the Pail on Substack (fillingthepail.substack.com), December 14, 2025
summary: Greg Ashman examines Sir Alan Wood's highly critical report on Mossbourne Victoria Park Academy as a case study in how reviews fail when they abandon natural justice. Although framed as a safeguarding practice review — a genre meant to learn lessons rather than apportion blame — Wood substantiates specific judgements of wrongdoing (shouting, public humiliation, a lack of reasonable adjustments) while refusing to put the details of complaints to the school so it could respond, violating the principle of Audi Alteram Partem. Ashman argues Wood repeatedly prefers negative evidence over positive: he dismisses his own largely positive survey, misapplies a statistical calculation to explain away self-selection bias in a 10% Ofsted survey, and reports SEND and ethnic 'disproportionality' against the school's own population rather than against comparable schools. Ashman concedes that if children were genuinely left to soil themselves or a culture of shouting was promoted, that is wrong and should be addressed — but concludes the report offers little more than the newspaper reports of a year earlier.
points: A safeguarding practice review is designed to learn lessons rather than apportion blame, so it does not follow natural justice — yet Wood used the format to substantiate specific findings of wrongdoing.
Wood did not put the details of complaints to the school, so it could not respond, violating Audi Alteram Partem (the right to hear the other side).
Wood gives 'more credence' to a self-selected 10% Ofsted survey and performs a statistical calculation that Ashman calls a basic error, since it cannot make sampling bias disappear.
Claims of disproportionality for SEND and ethnicity are measured against the school's own population, not against rates in comparable London schools, undermining the inference of discrimination.

Ashman notes a 'Heads I win; tails you lose' double-bind — the school is faulted both for dismissing mental-health concerns and for recording large numbers of them — while conceding genuine wrongdoing, if proven, should be addressed.
quotes: A key principle of natural justice is Audi Alteram Partem and requires that the details of allegations are put to the accused and that the accused is then given the opportunity to relate their own version of events. This was not honoured in Wood’s review.
It takes a serious act of doublethink to agree with Wood that he is not holding ‘individuals, organisations, or agencies to account’.
If the sample is biased, you cannot make the bias go away like this. When the stakes are this high, such an error is unfortunate.
This leads me to wonder exactly how Mossbourne Victoria Park Academy is both dismissing mental health concerns and reporting large numbers of them. Heads I win; tails you lose.
This is not because schools are discriminating, but because problematic behaviour is often a key criterion in diagnosing SEND.
However, if children have been regularly left to soil themselves, or if a culture of shouting and ‘healthy fear’ have been promoted by the school, then this is wrong and should be addressed.
The problem with Wood’s report is that it offers us little more than the newspaper reports from twelve months ago.
